L25@P3: Foreword
L26@P3: In 2023, the Maasai Mara National Reserve will be celebrating 75 years since its establishment
L27@P3: back in 1948. It is especially appropriate that this historic milestone coincides with the release
L28@P3: of this M aasai M ara National Reserve 10-year management plan, the first stakeholder
L29@P3: developed and approved management plan for the Reserve in more than 40 years.
L30@P3: The Mara Reserve is at the heart of the Mara-Serengeti ecosystem and home to the Great
L31@P3: Wildebeest Migration, internationally recognised as one of the New Seven Wonders of the
L32@P3: World alongside other priceless world heritages such as the Polar Ice Caps and the Grand
L33@P3: Canyon. For those who know the ecosystem well, this accolade comes as no surprise because
L34@P3: the migration and the natural ecosystem that supports it is without doubt one of the most
L35@P3: spectacular and breath-taking natural phenomena on earth.
L36@P3: However, major threats loom that seriously threaten the long-term viability of the Reserve
L37@P3: and wider ecosystem. If the Reserve is to survive for another 75 years, we urgently need a
L38@P3: roadmap that will enable us all to confront the many challenges the Reserve now faces.
L39@P3: It is for this reason that Narok County is proud to unveil this new MMNR Management Plan.
L40@P3: Through a highly participatory process involving the local community, national and county
L41@P3: legislators, the tourism industry, ecologists, scientists and Reserve managers, the plan sets out
L42@P3: a stakeholder-agreed vision for the future of the Mara Reserve plus, in simple and unambiguous
L43@P3: terms that all can understand, the means to achieve that vision. In line with the global significance of the Reserve and the greater ecosystem, the plan sets out a comprehensive agenda
L44@P3: for strengthening the management of the Reserve, designed to ensure the survival of this
L45@P3: unique and priceless national heritage, and the continuing generation of optimal economic
L46@P3: benefits from the Reserve for the people of the Narok County in which the Reserve is located,
L47@P3: as well as for all Kenyans.
L48@P3: The Mara Reserve and the greater Mara-Serengeti Ecosystem has had an illustrious and successful past of which we can all be proud, but with the help of this new management plan, we
L49@P3: are now embarking on a new future for the Reserve – one which is both in tune with the
L50@P3: international significance of this natural spectacle, its economic importance to Kenya and
L51@P3: Narok County, as well as with the rapidly mounting threats to the area. To achieve this bright
L52@P3: new future in the face of the difficult challenges confronting the Reserve will require both bold
L53@P3: leadership and committed management. We look forward to the next 75 years of the Reserve
L54@P3: with optimism and excitement about all that will be achieved as the Reserve continues to fulfil
L55@P3: its vital role in the conservation of the Mara ecosystem.
L56@P3: Hon. Johnson Ole Sipitiek
L57@P3: County Executive Committee Member, Tourism & Wildlife

L87@P5: Executive Summary
L88@P5: The Maasai Mara National Reserve is today faced by unprecedented challenges. Inside the
L89@P5: Reserve, escalating pressures from tourism development and growing visitor numbers drawn
L90@P5: by the world-renown of the Reserve’s wildebeest migration and other exceptional natural
L91@P5: resources are leading to a decline in the quality of the tourism product, and to a deterioration
L92@P5: of the natural habitats on which the Reserve’s tourism product is based, which is in turn
L93@P5: leading to a major decline in several of the Reserve’s charismatic wildlife species. Outside the
L94@P5: Reserve, there is growing pressure from local communities to use the Reserve’s pastures and
L95@P5: water sources for livestock, because of the diminishing supplies of these resources in the
L96@P5: wider ecosystem and deteriorating community livelihoods.
L97@P5: Rapidly changing land-use in the Greater Mara Ecosystem and uncontrolled tourism infrastructure development is also leading to diminishing dispersal areas and migratory corridors for the
L98@P5: Reserve’s wildlife, and escalating poaching and human-wildlife conflict. In the face of all these
L99@P5: and other challenges, the Narok County government and the Reserve’s management has been
L100@P5: unable to respond adequately to the changing circumstances, lacking as it does a clear road
L101@P5: map for the future management of the Reserve in a changing world, and also lacking the financial resources, manpower and infrastructure to address the emerging challenges.
L102@P5: In response to these serious concerns about the future of the Reserve, the Narok and Trans
L103@P5: Mara County Councils (now succeeded by Narok County) together with the Mara Conservancy (which is responsible for managing the Mara Triangle section of the Reserve) resolved in
L104@P5: May 2007 to develop a new 10-year management plan for the Reserve, the first management
L105@P5: plan for the Reserve to be developed for more than 40 years.
L106@P5: The initial planning process, which was spread out over the period 2008-2012 was co-financed
L107@P5: by the two councils together with the Mara Conservancy and the African Wildlife Foundation
L108@P5: (AWF), who also provided technical support and facilitation for the planning process. The
L109@P5: Conservation Development Centre (CDC) was enlisted to facilitate the planning process and
L110@P5: to draft the eventual management plan, working hand-in-hand with Reserve managers and
L111@P5: stakeholders and under the oversight of a Core Planning Team made up of county representatives, key stakeholders and managers.
L112@P5: The finalisation of the plan was put on hold as a result of the dissolution of the county councils
L113@P5: in 2013. Subsequently, the Narok County, successor to the two former county councils, took
L114@P5: over responsibility for the development of the new management plan, which led to an intensive period of activity to update the draft management plan in 2015-2016. However, the planning work was again put on hold in the lead up to the 2017 general elections.
L115@P5: In August 2020, work again commenced on finalising the new management plan, prompted by
L116@P5: the major challenges to the MMNR caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, especially the impacts
L117@P5: on the Reserve’s economic viability as a result of the sudden collapse of tourism in the area.
L118@P5-6: While without doubt a major setback for the Reserve, the post-pandemic recovery period
L119@P6: vii
L120@P6: has provided a significant opportunity to put the management of the Reserve on a strong
L121@P6: footing for the future, and this management plan is designed to help fulfil this.
L122@P6: Final approval of the management plan was postponed as a result of the 2022 general elections,
L123@P6: but in early 2023 the new Narok County administration picked up the baton once again leading
L124@P6: to the final review and approval of the plan by Members of the Narok County Assembly at a
L125@P6: retreat held in early February 2023, followed by signing into law of the plan by the Narok
L126@P6: County Governor on 21
L127@P6: st February 2023.
L128@P6: The main aims of the new management plan are to:
L129@P6:  Ensure conservation of the Reserve’s globally significant biodiversity
L130@P6:  Maintain the role of the MMNR as the flagship of Kenya’s tourism industry
L131@P6:  Improve on a sustainable basis the revenues generated by the MMNR, to support increasing community livelihood and PA management needs
L132@P6:  Provide a practical management framework to support MMNR managers in carrying
L133@P6: out their day-to-day management responsibilities.
L134@P6: In order to achieve these aims, the new plan sets out a set of stakeholder and management
L135@P6: agreed goals (the purpose statements and objectives) that Reserve managers will aim to
L136@P6: achieve, and a series of prescriptions and management actions that will be implemented in
L137@P6: order to ensure these goals are achieved. The plan mainly focuses on the management of the
L138@P6: Reserve itself, although to a limited degree it also addresses issues beyond the Reserve that
L139@P6: are impacting on the area, such as regarding ecological and community issues.
L140@P6: At the heart of the plan are the Visitor Carrying Capacity and Zonation and Visitor Use
L141@P6: Scheme chapters and the four management programmes, each of which cover an essential
L142@P6: aspect of reserve management. These four programmes are: the Ecological Management Programme, the Tourism Management Programme, the Community Outreach & Partnership Programme, and the Protected Area Operations Programme

L155@P7: An important aspect of the new plan is that it aims to provide a mechanism for managing the
L156@P7: MMNR as a single visitor destination and ecological unit. Over the years, the management
L157@P7: of the Central Mara (Narok) and Mara Triangle sections of the Reserve have gradually diverged, to the extent that today there are significant differences on both sides of the Reserve,
L158@P7: which leads to confusion amongst the area’s users and inefficiencies in the use of management
L159@P7: resources. One of the key underlying principles in developing this management plan was therefore to bring the management of the two sides of the Reserve much closer together, through
L160@P7: coordinated and unified management based on a shared vision and objectives, and common
L161@P7: management action priorities.

L711@P23: 2.1 History and purpose
L712@P23: The Maasai Mara National Reserve was first established in
L713@P23: 1948, when the Mara Triangle,
L714@P23: a 520 km2area between the
L715@P23: Siria escarpment, the Tanzanian border and the Mara
L716@P23: River, was declared a National
L717@P23: Game Reserve. The Reserve
L718@P23: was primarily created to protect the spectacular wildlife of
L719@P23: the ecosystem. In 1961, the
L720@P23: Reserve was brought under
L721@P23: the control of the County
L722@P23: Council of Narok, and the
L723@P23: core area was extended to
L724@P23: the east to encompass an area
L725@P23: of 1,831 square kilometres. In
L726@P23: 1984, parts of Reserve were excised to provide access to watering points for livestock, and
L727@P23: the Reserve was brought to its present size of 1,530 square kilometres, as shown in Figure 1
L728@P23: above.
L729@P23: In 1995, following the creation of the Trans Mara District, the management of the Reserve
L730@P23: was split between the County Councils of Narok and Trans Mara, with CCN responsible for
L731@P23: the Reserve to the east of the Mara River, and CCTM responsible for the Reserve to the west
L732@P23: of the river (known as the Mara Triangle). In 2001, the day-to-day management of the Mara
L733@P23: Triangle was contracted to an independent non-profit protected area management company,
L734@P23: the M ara Conservancy, under an initial five-year management agreement. This management
L735@P23: agreement has been subsequently extended.
L736@P23: In 2013, as part of the constitutional reforms to Kenya local government, the two county
L737@P23: councils were superseded by the Narok County, which is now responsible for the management of the entire Reserve. However, the Mara Conservancy still manages the Mara Triangle
L738@P23: on behalf of Narok County and, under a recently endorsed collaboration agreement with the
L739@P23: County, is playing an increasing role in bringing about the unified management of the entire
L740@P23: Reserve.
L741@P23: Despite these changes in the size and management of the Reserve in the 75 years since the
L742@P23: area’s initial gazettement, the MMNR has throughout this time provided a vital refuge for
L743@P23: wildlife, most notably the elephant and Black rhino populations, and for the spectacular annual

L752@P24: However, it is important to recognise that the Mara National Reserve is primarily established
L753@P24: as a crucial Kenya wildlife conservation area, and only secondarily as a tourism destination.
L754@P24: From the outset, tourism in the MMNR has always played a supportive role to the Reserve’s
L755@P24: primary conservation purpose - facilitating the management of the Reserve and the conservation of its biodiversity through the provision of revenues, and enabling visitors, both Kenyan
L756@P24: and international, to appreciate and enjoy the biodiversity and habitats for which the MMNR
L757@P24: is justly renowned.
L758@P24: These major functions that the Reserve has played correspond with oral testimony given by
L759@P24: local residents on the reasons the Reserve was gazetted, which states: “it was the intention
L760@P24: that the game reserve should be Maasai owned. The idea was for African participation and to

L763@P24: .
L764@P24: As its name suggests, the Maasai Mara National Reserve is therefore unique amongst Kenya’s
L765@P24: protected areas in its role as a cultural and natural heritage of the Maasai. The purpose that
L766@P24: the MMNR serves is not simply to provide a sanctuary for wildlife and revenue generation
L767@P24: through tourism, but also as a living and vivid testimony to the Maasai’s traditional conservation-compatible and wildlife tolerant pastoralist livelihood. Since the Maasai communities’ traditional land use practices are responsible for the preservation of the Reserve’s exceptional
L768@P24: natural resources in the first place, it is also important that the benefits that are now being
L769@P24: derived from these resources are first and foremost channelled back to these communities.
L770@P24: In short, the purpose of the Reserve can be summarised as:
L771@P24: The Maasai Mara National Reserve is the keystone of the greater MaraSerengeti Ecosystem, a safe haven for the great migration, a powerhouse of
L772@P24: sustainable economic benefits, and a living testimony to the Maasai
L773@P24: community’s conservation ideals and affinity with wildlife.
L774@P24: This purpose is further elaborated in the individual programme purpose statements which are
L775@P24: provided at the beginning of each of the four management programmes.

L3858@P109: Action 1.7 Support measures to have the MMNR recognised as a World Heritage Site

L3860@P109: the World - the Great Migration - unlike the neighbouring Serengeti National Park, the Reserve has not yet been recognised as a World Heritage Site. The addition of the Reserve to
L3861@P109: the list of World Heritage Sites is vital for the future conservation of the Reserve’s biodiversity
L3862@P109: and habitats and will also promote the Reserve as a visitor destination. In this regard, the initial
L3863@P109: application to add the MMNR to the World Heritage List was made by KWS in 2010, and the
L3864@P109: Reserve is currently on the tentative list of future World Heritage Sites.
